notes: Complete joint EWCA Civ judgment on lawfulness of detaining asylum seekers who had notified intention to seek judicial review.

enrichment.short_title: Asylum seeker detention unlawful where unpublished policy ignored credible notice of impending judicial review
key_facts: Two Sri Lankan asylum seekers (N and A) were detained by the Secretary of State on the ground that removal was imminent, although each had notified the Home Office of an intention to challenge removal.
N was detained before judicial review was lodged; A was detained after refusing to cooperate with Sri Lankan High Commission documentation while intending to appeal under section 65.
High Court judges held both detentions unlawful; the Secretary of State appealed on the lawfulness of his detention policy.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consolidated appeals to the Court of Appeal against High Court declarations that detention of two asylum seekers was unlawful.
enrichment.outcome: Secretary of State's appeals dismissed; detentions held unlawful and damages claims remitted for assessment.
enrichment.ratio: Where proceedings challenging removal have been initiated, removal is not treated as imminent and detention for removal alone is normally unjustified; the Secretary of State may lawfully disregard mere intimations of future proceedings when assessing imminence, but that unpublished aspect of policy was not accessible or foreseeable and could not render detention lawful where published policy indicated otherwise.
legal_issues: Whether detention was lawful where removal was said to be imminent but judicial review or appeal was about to be commenced
What the Secretary of State's published and unpublished detention policies were
Whether disregarding credible notice of impending proceedings was arbitrary or irrational
Whether detention complied with Article 5(1)(f) and the requirement that deprivation of liberty be prescribed by accessible law

notes: Complete EWCA Civ judgment giving guidance on CPR 43 PD 6.6 and costs estimates at assessment.

enrichment.short_title: Costs estimates under CPR 43 PD 6.6 are not binding caps where paying party did not rely on them
key_facts: Claimant's solicitors estimated future profit costs at £3,000 in the allocation questionnaire but ultimately claimed about £14,500 in profit costs on assessment after settlement.
The defendant argued the claimant should recover no more than the estimate plus 15%, or at least that the estimate should reduce assessed costs.
District and circuit judges refused to cap costs by reference to the estimate; the defendant appealed on a point of principle.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal from a circuit judge's refusal to interfere with a district judge's detailed assessment of costs.
enrichment.ratio: CPR 43 PD 6.6 permits the court to have regard to costs estimates as one factor among others when assessing reasonableness, but a party should not be bound to an inadequate estimate simply as a penalty; reductions are appropriate where the paying party relied on the estimate, different case management would likely have followed a realistic estimate, or the difference is unexplained—estimates are not retrospective budgets or caps.
legal_issues: Whether CPR 43 PD 6.6 makes a costs estimate a cap on recoverable costs
How courts should take account of substantial divergence between estimate and final bill
Whether practice directions can affect assessment criteria under CPR r 44.5
Application of the indemnity principle and Wong v Vizards

notes: Complete High Court statutory appeal on adequacy of GMC Committee on Professional Performance reasons.

enrichment.short_title: GMC suspension extension upheld despite failure to mention supportive GP tutor evidence in reasons
key_facts: GP Dr Krishnamurthy was suspended for 12 months in 2002 after a performance assessment found serious deficiencies in clinical practice and record keeping.
Before a review hearing in July 2003 he undertook educational steps including work with Dr Bailey and GP tutor Dr Adams, who recommended supervised clinical practice.
The Committee extended suspension for a further 12 months without expressly addressing Dr Adams' evidence, finding continued lack of insight and risk to patient safety.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Statutory appeal under section 40(1)(aa) of the Medical Act 1983 against a GMC Committee on Professional Performance decision extending suspension.
enrichment.ratio: A Committee on Professional Performance need not expressly reject evidence central to the practitioner's case where its decision clearly explains why the practitioner's performance remains deficient; a brief regulatory determination is not required to be a fully reasoned judgment, and failure to mention Dr Adams' views was not fatal when the reasons showed the committee had assessed the overall evidence differently on fuller material.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee erred in law by failing to mention or explain rejection of Dr Adams' evidence
Minimum standards of reasons in GMC performance proceedings
Whether delay in implementing educational advice and preparing a personal learning plan supported extension of suspension
Whether a further performance assessment requirement was unreasonable after prolonged suspension

notes: Complete EWCA Civ judgment applying Qazi to article 8 defence in local authority possession proceedings.

enrichment.short_title: Article 8 cannot defeat council possession after estranged wife's valid notice to quit (post-Qazi)
key_facts: Mr Kibata remained in a Newham flat after his estranged wife, alleging domestic violence, served a valid notice to quit as a condition of being re-housed under the council's domestic violence policy.
The county court dismissed the possession claim, finding article 8(2) justification lacking and criticising the council's conduct in procuring the notice to quit.
Following Qazi v London Borough of Harrow, the Court of Appeal held article 8 unavailable as a defence where the occupier had no domestic law right to remain.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal to the Court of Appeal from a county court refusal to grant possession, heard after the House of Lords decision in Qazi.
enrichment.outcome: Council's appeal allowed and possession order made; cross-appeal on articles 6 and 14 dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: After a valid tenant's notice to quit terminates the tenancy, a local authority entitled to immediate possession as freeholder may enforce that right without a county court undertaking an article 8(2) proportionality inquiry; article 8 does not create a possessory right defeating ordinary proprietary rights, and public law challenges to the authority's conduct belong in judicial review unless wholly exceptional.
legal_issues: Whether article 8 provides a defence to possession proceedings after termination of secure tenancy
Effect of Qazi on county court possession claims against trespassing occupiers
Whether the council unlawfully procured a notice to quit to avoid domestic violence possession safeguards
Whether articles 6 and 14 were engaged by the council's housing policy

notes: Complete EWCA Civ judgment in paired Birmingham possession appeals applying Qazi.

enrichment.short_title: Bradney and McCann: article 8 rejected as defence to Birmingham council possession after joint tenant notice to quit
key_facts: In Bradney, a joint tenant signed a notice to quit intending to protect the remaining occupier but effectively terminating the joint tenancy; the county court granted possession after an article 8(2) inquiry.
In McCann, the council obtained a notice to quit from a joint tenant following domestic violence re-housing; the county court dismissed possession proceedings on article 8 grounds.
Both occupiers had no remaining tenancy rights and relied solely on article 8 after Qazi.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Two related appeals to the Court of Appeal from Birmingham County Court possession decisions, heard alongside Newham v Kibata.
enrichment.outcome: Bradney appeal dismissed; McCann appeal allowed and possession order made.
enrichment.ratio: Following Qazi, article 8 is not available as a defence to possession proceedings brought to enforce a local authority's ordinary property rights after a valid notice to quit, even where the premises are the occupier's home and the council encouraged the notice; circumventing section 82 procedures is not established merely because the council instigated the tenant's notice.
legal_issues: Whether article 8 permits refusal of a possession order where domestic law rights have ended
Whether councils act unlawfully by obtaining notices to quit from joint tenants in domestic violence cases
Whether Bradney or McCann are distinguishable from Qazi on the facts
Role of judicial review versus article 8 in county court possession claims

enrichment.short_title: Conditional permission granted on meaning of 'required' for Kent County Council standby duty pay
key_facts: Mr Grant, manager of out-of-hours social services, worked extensive standby hours beyond his 37-hour week without standby duty allowance.
The employment tribunal held the work was a moral rather than contractual requirement and not 'required' under the Blue Book terms.
The EAT held 'required' included work necessary in the absence of other cover or expected by the council, and remitted the case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal from an Employment Appeal Tribunal decision.

enrichment.ratio: 'Required' in the Blue Book standby allowance provision is not limited to express contractual or managerial direction; work necessary to keep the out-of-hours service operating, or expected by the council in the absence of other staff, can suffice, though the EAT's 'expected by the Council' limb may create uncertainty warranting further appellate consideration.

enrichment.short_title: Aircraft hanger at King's Farm held not Class E permitted development incidental to dwellinghouse enjoyment

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (General Permitted Development) Order 1995

key_facts: Mr Holding kept four private aircraft at King's Farm, Orsett, using a large hanger and hardstanding subject to enforcement notice 3.
An inspector refused planning permission and dismissed the enforcement appeal, finding the hanger was not required for a purpose incidental to enjoyment of the dwellinghouse.
The appellant argued personal flying use was incidental and that the inspector inconsistently accepted flying as ancillary in an earlier notice decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal under section 289 of the Town and Country Planning Act 1990 against an inspector's decision on enforcement notice 3 and related deemed planning applications.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; permission to appeal to Court of Appeal refused; Secretary of State awarded £6,885 costs.
enrichment.ratio: Whether a building is required for a purpose incidental to enjoyment of the particular dwellinghouse is judged objectively by fact and degree, taking account of normal residential uses but focusing on the specific property; a further large hanger for three aircraft went beyond what could reasonably be regarded as incidental, and the inspector's earlier finding on flying use did not bind the separate Class E building test.

Whether the objective test looks at dwellinghouses generally or the particular dwelling

enrichment.short_title: Buyer failed to prove developer repudiated NHBC contract over lower-ground-floor tanking remedial scheme
key_facts: Mr Skinner contracted to buy a new Type H house at St Luke's Park, Guildford, but refused completion after Crest Nicholson carried out remedial waterproofing to the lower ground floor using Hey'di tanking and inner blockwork.
The buyer claimed the remedial scheme altered drawings/specifications without consent and meant the house was not built in a good and workmanlike manner, repudiating the NHBC-style contract.
The house was later sold to another buyer at a discounted price; Crest counterclaimed for unpaid deposit balance.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial in the Technology and Construction Court of buyer's claim and developer's counterclaim for deposit forfeiture.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; judgment for Crest on counterclaim for £19,250 plus interest; developer discharged from obligation to sell and buyer forfeited deposit paid.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 3.2 of the NHBC contract referred only to drawings and specifications provided in the Home Manual, not internal construction drawings; the remedial scheme did not diminish value and did not mean the completed house failed the implied good and workmanlike standard, so the developer did not repudiate and the buyer was in breach for failing to complete.
legal_issues: Whether remedial waterproofing works constituted an impermissible variation under clause 3.2
Whether completion of the remedial scheme meant the house was not built in a good and workmanlike manner

notes: Complete judicial review on lawfulness of section 50 Mental Health Act remittal of life-sentenced patient to prison.

enrichment.short_title: Section 50 MHA remittal to prison upheld; RMO recommendation not challengeable on Convention grounds alone
key_facts: The claimant was convicted of manslaughter, sentenced to life with an eight-year tariff, and transferred to hospital under sections 47/49 after psychotic deterioration in prison.
The RMO notified under section 50(1) that he no longer required hospital treatment; the Secretary of State decided to remit him to HMP Cardiff.
The claimant sought to block return to prison alleging Articles 3 and 5 violations and challenging the RMO's clinical recommendation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review and Human Rights Act claim with interim injunction restraining return to prison.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to apply for judicial review against RMO refused; substantive claim against Secretary of State dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A responsible medical officer's section 50(1) notification is a clinical judgment reviewable for rationality and fairness but not challengeable on Convention grounds because any Convention breach arises only if the Secretary of State acts on it; Article 5(4) is not engaged by a decision to move a lawfully detained prisoner from hospital to prison, and remittal does not violate Articles 3 or 5 unless it is clear that future prison treatment will be inhuman or that detention as mentally unsound must continue in a suitable therapeutic environment.
legal_issues: Whether section 50(1) is incompatible with Article 5(4)
Whether remittal to prison violates Article 5(1)(e) while mental illness persists
Whether return to prison would breach Article 3 given risk of relapse and past delays in readmission
